:::{#thm-pd-gram}
#### Definite matrices are Gram matrices

Let $\matr{A}$ be a $p \times p$ matrix.

1. $\matr{A}$ is positive semidefinite (@def-positive-semidefinite)
   exactly when $\matr{A} = \tp{\matr{B}} \matr{B}$ for some matrix $\matr{B}$ with $p$ columns.
2. $\matr{A}$ is positive definite (@def-positive-definite)
   exactly when $\matr{A} = \tp{\matr{B}} \matr{B}$ for some matrix $\matr{B}$
   with $p$ linearly independent columns.

:::

::: proof

**If $\matr{A} = \tp{\matr{B}} \matr{B}$.**
$\matr{A}$ is symmetric, since
$\tp{(\tp{\matr{B}} \matr{B})} = \tp{\matr{B}}\,\tp{(\tp{\matr{B}})} = \tp{\matr{B}} \matr{B}$
(@thm-transpose-product, @def-matrix-transpose). For any $\vx$,

$$
\ba
\tp{\vx} \matr{A} \vx
&= \tp{\vx}\,\tp{\matr{B}}\,\matr{B} \vx
&& \text{(substitute } \matr{A} \text{)}
\\
&= \tp{(\matr{B} \vx)}\,(\matr{B} \vx)
&& \text{(@thm-transpose-product, @thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \norm{\matr{B} \vx}^2
&& \text{(@eq-l2-norm, squared)}
\\
&\ge 0.
&& \text{(@thm-norm-properties)}
\ea
$$

If the columns of $\matr{B}$ are linearly independent,
then $\mathcal{N}(\matr{B}) = \cb{\vzero}$
($\matr{B} \vx$ is the combination of the columns with coefficients $x_j$, @thm-matvec-columns,
and only the zero combination is $\vzero$, @def-linearly-independent),
so for $\vx \ne \vzero$, $\matr{B} \vx \ne \vzero$ and $\norm{\matr{B} \vx}^2 > 0$
(@thm-norm-properties, part 1).

**Only if.**
Let $\matr{A}$ be positive semidefinite.
It is symmetric, so $\matr{A} = \matr{Q} \matr{\Lambda} \tp{\matr{Q}}$ (@thm-spectral),
and every $\lambda_i \ge 0$ (@thm-definite-eigenvalues).
Let $\matr{\Lambda}^{1/2} \eqdef \diag(\sqrt{\lambda_1}, \ldots, \sqrt{\lambda_p})$,
which is symmetric, with $\matr{\Lambda}^{1/2} \matr{\Lambda}^{1/2} = \matr{\Lambda}$
(the product of diagonal matrices multiplies their diagonals, as in the proof of @thm-diagonalizable-powers),
and let $\matr{B} \eqdef \matr{\Lambda}^{1/2} \tp{\matr{Q}}$. Then

$$
\ba
\tp{\matr{B}} \matr{B}
&= \tp{(\tp{\matr{Q}})}\,\tp{(\matr{\Lambda}^{1/2})}\,\matr{\Lambda}^{1/2} \tp{\matr{Q}}
&& \text{(@thm-transpose-product)}
\\
&= \matr{Q}\,\matr{\Lambda}^{1/2} \matr{\Lambda}^{1/2}\,\tp{\matr{Q}}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-transpose; } \matr{\Lambda}^{1/2} \text{ is symmetric)}
\\
&= \matr{Q} \matr{\Lambda} \tp{\matr{Q}}
&& \text{(} \matr{\Lambda}^{1/2} \matr{\Lambda}^{1/2} = \matr{\Lambda} \text{)}
\\
&= \matr{A}.
&& \text{(@thm-spectral)}
\ea
$$

If $\matr{A}$ is positive definite, it is positive semidefinite (@rem-positive-definite-symmetry),
so the same $\matr{B}$ gives $\matr{A} = \tp{\matr{B}} \matr{B}$; and every $\lambda_i > 0$ (@thm-definite-eigenvalues),
so $\matr{\Lambda}^{1/2}$ is diagonal with nonzero diagonal, and invertible
(its inverse is $\diag(1/\sqrt{\lambda_1}, \ldots, 1/\sqrt{\lambda_p})$);
$\tp{\matr{Q}}$ is invertible with inverse $\matr{Q}$ (@rem-orthogonal-matrix-columns).
So $\matr{B}$ is invertible (@thm-inverse-product),
and its $p$ columns are linearly independent (@thm-invertible-rank, @def-rank).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-pd-gram}
#### Gram factorizations

- With $\matr{R} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ ($1 \times 2$),
  $\tp{\matr{R}} \matr{R} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$,
  the positive semidefinite matrix of @exm-positive-semidefinite;
  the two columns of $\matr{R}$, $1$ and $1$, are dependent, so part 2 does not apply to $\matr{R}$;
  $\tp{\matr{R}} \matr{R}$ is in fact not positive definite (@exm-positive-definite).
- With $\mX = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$, whose columns are independent (@exm-rank),
  $\tp{\mX} \mX = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ 6 & 14 \end{bmatrix}$ (@exm-gram-invertible)
  is positive definite.
- $\matr{D} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ of @exm-positive-definite is symmetric
  but not positive semidefinite, so by part 1 it is not $\tp{\matr{B}} \matr{B}$ for any $\matr{B}$.

:::
